strengths: The combination of multilevel Monte Carlo and Stein control functionals is well motivated. It can exploit inexpensive approximations while accommodating unnormalized target densities when scores are available.

The sample-split integration estimator has a clear unbiasedness argument. The variance bound and explicit allocation rule provide useful insight into the roles of smoothness, dimension, and evaluation cost.

The experiments report promising integration-error reductions over CF and MLMC, with 50–100 repetitions for integration examples, an ecological posterior application, and additional kernel and sample-allocation comparisons.
weaknesses: The variational-inference experiments contain a central unresolved inconsistency. Appendix D.5 repeatedly specifies one sample for MLCFRG. With one total observation, Equation (11) reduces exactly to the observed gradient difference and becomes independent of the kernel; the sample-split estimator cannot be constructed either. Consequently, the reported control-functional gains and kernel comparisons require an explanation of any additional fitting observations, their reuse, and their cost.

The VI theoretical claims exceed the proof. Although the text acknowledges that Proposition 3.4 is conditional, Appendix B.5 removes the previous update from the variance without establishing control of accumulated gradient error. Theorem 3.2 concerns fixed integrands and independent levels; its extension to adaptive optimization histories is not proved. Furthermore, its global fill-distance assumption cannot hold on the Gaussian domains used experimentally, and the ReLU examples lack the required smoothness justification.

Appendix C.1 gives an incorrect multidimensional Matérn mixed-derivative trace: the first two terms require a factor of d. At coincident inputs, the trace should equal 5dσ²/(3λ²), whereas the printed expression is dimension-independent. This matters for the two-dimensional synthetic experiment because using that expression would compromise the Stein-kernel construction. The manuscript does not establish whether this is only a transcription error.

The boundary-value ODE benchmark needs a well-posedness justification. Gaussian x1 allows c(z)=1+x1z to vanish inside the domain, so positive diffusivity and existence of the intended solution are not guaranteed. Appendix D.3 also changes the forcing from −50²x2² to +50x2² during expansion. These discrepancies leave the actual numerical target uncertain.

The efficiency claims lack complete computational accounting. The allocation budget covers sampling/function evaluations but omits cubic kernel solves, hyperparameter fitting, and allocation overhead. These costs cannot simply be assumed negligible for the reported millisecond evaluations. BNN curves against iterations, with different sample counts across methods, also do not establish an improvement in elapsed time.

The methodological advance is largely a composition of established CF and MLMC constructions, with the allocation obtained by optimizing the inherited bound. Its practical value needs stronger comparative evidence: the proposed allocation is tested only on a tailored example with known RKHS norms; multilevel Bayesian quadrature is omitted in tractable settings; QMC is not matched across competing integration methods; and VI lacks a single-level CF baseline. One subsampled UCI dataset with small networks provides limited evidence of broader AI significance.

Important reproduction details are missing: which experiments use the unbiased versus simplified estimator, fitting/evaluation splits, reference-integral computation and accuracy, actual ODE/Lotka–Volterra level resolutions, MCMC diagnostics, and the BNN subset and train/test split. The relationship between the SGD-specific recursion and the reported Adam implementation is also unexplained. These omissions make the numerical and theoretical discrepancies difficult to resolve.
